624.title: Holy, holy, holy (Apocalypse 4)
624.hook: around the throne the living creatures never stop singing
624.howItsDone: At every Mass, at the end of the Preface, the priest invites the people to join the angels and saints, and all sing or say the Sanctus, Holy, Holy, Holy, drawn from Isaiah 6 and Apocalypse 4.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lantern at the overgrown door. Your line was I stand and knock. Did a door remind you of him today? Day six hundred twenty-four.

Yesterday, Christ stood outside a door, knocking. Chapter four turns the picture around. John writes: "behold a door was opened in heaven." A voice like a trumpet says, come up here. And suddenly John isn't looking at seven small churches in Asia anymore. He's looking through a doorway into the center of everything. Until now the Apocalypse has kept its eyes on earth. Here the camera swings up. What John sees first isn't a battle, or a beast, or a timeline. It's worship.
screen: `A DOOR OPENED IN HEAVEN.` → `COME UP HITHER.` → `THE CENTER OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: John tries to describe the throne, and you can feel him reaching for words. The one seated there looks like jasper and sardine stone. A rainbow like emerald circles the throne. Lightning, thunder, seven burning lamps, and before it a sea of glass like crystal. Around it sit twenty-four elders in white, with gold crowns. And close around the throne, four living creatures: one like a lion, one like a calf, one with a man's face, one like a flying eagle. Each has six wings and is covered with eyes. Then the sound. In the Douay-Rheims: "And they rested not day and night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come." Rested not. That's today's line. The song never stops. John's readers would have heard an echo. Long before, in the temple, the prophet Isaiah saw the seraphim crying to each other: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." Holy is often explained as set apart, other, nothing like us. Saying it three times piles it up as high as the words will go. Then the twenty-four elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne. Every honor they have, they give back. Catholics know this song. At every Mass, at the end of the Preface, the priest says that we join the angels and saints in their hymn, and the people sing the Sanctus: holy, holy, holy. That's not decoration. The Church says the Mass on earth joins the worship John saw through that open door. Later Christian tradition made the four creatures symbols of the four Gospel writers: Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the calf, John the eagle.
screen: `JASPER, EMERALD, A SEA OF GLASS.` · `FOUR LIVING CREATURES.` · `ISAIAH HEARD IT TOO.` · `THE SANCTUS AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, LORD GOD ALMIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: join the song, here, quietly. Sit comfortably and breathe. Picture what John saw: the door open in heaven, the rainbow, the sea of glass, the creatures with their wings, the elders laying down their crowns. Let it be bright and loud in your mind. Then imagine that the song has been going on the whole time, through every ordinary minute of your day. If you pray, you can join it softly: holy, holy, holy, once on each out-breath. If you don't, just listen in your imagination to a song that never rests. The next time you're at Mass, listen for the moment it begins. The bell holds the time.
Holy. Set apart, wholly other. Sung three times by the creatures around the throne, and by the people at every Mass. Today's word.
Your line: they rest not. Today, once, at an ordinary moment, stop and remember the song that's still going. Day six hundred twenty-four.

625.title: The Lamb that was slain (Apocalypse 5)
625.hook: the Mass joins this heavenly liturgy (CCC 1090)
625.howItsDone: At every Mass, while the host is broken, the people sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, three times, and the priest then shows the host with the words of John the Baptist, Behold the Lamb of God; the Church teaches that the earthly liturgy shares in the heavenly one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the door opened in heaven, and holy, holy, holy. Your line was they rest not. When did you remember the song that never stops? Day six hundred twenty-five.

The Hallelujah chorus is where audiences stand up during Handel's Messiah. It isn't the ending. The Hallelujah comes at the end of the second part. The whole work closes later, with a slower, larger chorus, and then an Amen that goes on and on, voices climbing over each other for minutes. The words of that last chorus are worthy is the Lamb that was slain. They come from the fifth chapter of the Apocalypse, where they are sung in heaven, by a choir far bigger than any concert hall could hold.
screen: `NOT THE HALLELUJAH.` → `THE LAST CHORUS OF MESSIAH.` → `WORTHY IS THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Chapter five begins with a problem. In the right hand of the one on the throne is a scroll, written inside and out, sealed with seven seals. A strong angel calls out: who is worthy to open it? And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth can. John starts to cry. He weeps much, he says. Then one of the elders tells him, weep not: the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David, has won, and can open the scroll. So John turns to look for a lion. And what he sees is a Lamb. Standing, and yet looking as though it had been slain. You were told a lion; you see a lamb with its wounds still showing. That's the whole book in one image. The power that wins is a love that was killed and is alive. The Greek word John uses is arnion, which can mean a little lamb. The Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven erupts. The creatures and the elders fall down with harps and bowls of incense, which the text says are the prayers of the saints. Then thousands upon thousands of angels sing, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lamb that was slain is worthy to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and benediction." Then every creature, in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, joins in. Catholics hear this at Mass. As the host is broken before Communion, the people sing or say the Lamb of God, and the priest holds up the host and says, behold the Lamb of God. The Catechism says that in the liturgy on earth, the Church already shares in this heavenly one.
screen: `A SCROLL NO ONE CAN OPEN.` · `TOLD A LION, JOHN SEES A LAMB.` · `THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS.` · `THE LAMB OF GOD AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THE LAMB THAT WAS SLAIN IS WORTHY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the Agnus Dei, or sit with it. Settle, and breathe. Picture the scene: the throne, the scroll, the Lamb standing with its wounds showing, and every creature everywhere singing. Let your own small voice be one of them. If you pray, you can say the Agnus Dei slowly, old words of the Mass, in your own language or in the old Latin: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Say it three times, slowly, a breath for each. If you don't pray, just picture the Lamb, and notice what it means that the winner has wounds. The bell holds the time.
Arnion, a little lamb. Apocalypse five: the lamb standing with its wounds still showing, worthy to open the scroll no one else could open. Today's word.
Your line: worthy is the lamb. Today, the next time you're at Mass or hear the Lamb of God, remember the scroll and the song. Day six hundred twenty-five.

626.title: A great multitude (Apocalypse 7:9–17)
626.hook: from all nations, tribes, peoples and tongues; read on All Saints
626.tomorrow: a woman clothed with the sun
626.howItsDone: On the Solemnity of All Saints, November 1, Catholics hear Apocalypse 7 at Mass and honor all the saints, known and unknown; the next day, All Souls, they pray for all the faithful departed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arnion, standing with its wounds still showing. Your line was worthy is the lamb. Did you hear the Lamb of God differently? Day six hundred twenty-six.

On the first of November, the Church celebrates All Saints. Not one saint. All of them. The famous ones with feast days and statues, yes, but also the ones nobody ever canonized: the grandmother who prayed the rosary on the bus, the farmer who never missed Sunday, the nurse who held hands on night shifts. Names no calendar has room for. The first reading at Mass that day comes from Apocalypse seven. It begins with a number, and then John looks up and sees something no number can hold.
screen: `THE FIRST OF NOVEMBER.` → `SAINTS NO CALENDAR CAN HOLD.` → `A NUMBER, THEN A CROWD.`

segments.voice: First John hears a number: a hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel. Twelve times twelve, times a thousand: Catholic interpreters read it as a symbol of the whole people of God, complete. And then, just as he heard of a lion and saw a lamb, he hears a number and sees a crowd. In the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." Every tongue. Every accent and alphabet on earth, standing together. Palms in their hands, a sign of victory, like the crowd that waved branches when Jesus rode into Jerusalem. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. Then one of the elders asks John a question he can't answer: who are these in white, and where did they come from? And John, overwhelmed, says simply, "My lord, thou knowest." The elder tells him: "These are they who are come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and have made them white in the blood of the Lamb." Robes washed in blood come out white. It's meant to stop you. These aren't people who avoided suffering. They came through it. And the chapter ends with a promise for them: no more hunger, no more thirst, no burning sun. The Lamb will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water. On All Saints, Catholics remember that this crowd includes people they knew.
screen: `A NUMBER: 144,000.` · `A CROWD NO MAN COULD NUMBER.` · `MY LORD, THOU KNOWEST.` · `WASHED WHITE IN THE BLOOD OF THE LAMB.` · then, large: `ALL NATIONS, AND TRIBES, AND PEOPLES, AND TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture that crowd. Close your eyes if you like, and breathe. Imagine a huge open space in front of a throne, and people arriving. Faces from every continent. Old women in headscarves, teenagers, farmers, a child holding a palm branch, a man in a wheelchair, languages you don't know. Let it fill up until you can't see the edges. Now look for someone you knew: a grandparent, a friend, a teacher who has died. Find them in the crowd, in white, holding a palm. If you pray, you can ask them to pray for you. If you don't, just let yourself see them there. The bell holds the time.
A great multitude. Apocalypse seven: a crowd no one could count, from every nation and tongue, in white before the Lamb. Today's word.
Your line: every tongue. Today, when you hear a language you don't understand, picture its speakers in that crowd. Day six hundred twenty-six.

627.title: A woman clothed with the sun (Apocalypse 12)
627.hook: the moon under her feet and twelve stars; read on the Assumption as Mary and the Church
627.howItsDone: Catholics hear Apocalypse 12 on the Solemnity of the Assumption, August 15, and Marian art, especially images of the Immaculate Conception, often shows Mary with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great multitude, from every nation, in white, with palms. Your line was every tongue. Whose language did you picture in that crowd? Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Nearly six hundred years before Christ, Babylon's army burned the temple in Jerusalem. After that, the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, is never seen again in the Bible's history. Nobody knows what became of it. One old story, in Second Maccabees, says the prophet Jeremiah hid it in a cave on a mountain until God gathers his people again. Then, at the very end of Apocalypse eleven, John sees God's temple in heaven open, and there it is: the ark. And the very next thing he sees isn't a chest at all. It's a woman.
screen: `THE ARK, LOST WITH THE TEMPLE.` → `SEEN AGAIN IN HEAVEN.` → `THEN, A WOMAN.`

segments.voice: Right after the ark, in the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." She is about to give birth, crying out in pain. And a second sign appears: a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, standing in front of her, waiting to devour the child as soon as it's born. The child is born, a son who will rule all the nations, and he's caught up to God and to his throne. The woman flees into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared for her. Then war breaks out in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon, and the dragon is thrown down. The text names him: that old serpent, the devil. That old serpent takes us all the way back to Genesis, where God tells the serpent there will be enmity between him and the woman, between his seed and hers. Who is the woman? Catholic tradition doesn't pick just one answer. She is Mary, who bore the child who rules the nations; the Church reads this passage on the feast of the Assumption, in August. She is also the Church, the people of God, who bring Christ into the world in pain and are kept safe in the wilderness. And many readers also see Israel in her twelve stars, the twelve tribes. The symbols carry more than one meaning at once. Notice how the scene began: with the ark of the covenant. Catholic tradition has long called Mary the ark of the new covenant, the one who carried God within her.
screen: `THE ARK SEEN IN HEAVEN.` · `A WOMAN, A CHILD, A DRAGON.` · `THAT OLD SERPENT, FROM GENESIS.` · `MARY, THE CHURCH, AND ISRAEL.` · then, large: `A WOMAN CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the moon, or picture it. If it's evening and the moon is up, go to a window or step outside. If not, close your eyes and picture it, the way you've seen it on a clear night. Breathe. Imagine the moon under someone's feet, as if it were a footstool. Then the sun around her, and twelve stars over her head. Let the size of it land: the whole sky as clothing. Then remember that she was also a mother in pain, with a dragon in front of her, and she was kept safe. If you pray, you can ask Mary to pray for you. If you don't, just stay with the sky. The bell holds the time.
Michael, the archangel. Apocalypse twelve: he and his angels throw the ancient dragon, that old serpent, out of heaven. Today's word.
Your line: clothed with the sun. Tonight, look for the moon, and if you find it, remember the woman standing on it. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

628.title: Babylon falls (Apocalypse 18)
628.hook: the merchants weep over a city built on luxury
628.howItsDone: Catholic social teaching warns against consumerism and insists that people are never merchandise; Catholics practice simplicity through fasting and almsgiving, especially in Lent, and support fair labor and the fight against human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman with the moon under her feet. Your line was clothed with the sun. Did you find the moon last night? Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Open a shopping app and scroll. Gold jewelry. Silk scarves. Rare wood furniture. Perfume. Fine wine. Imported spices. Grass-fed beef. A car. Everything delivered to your door, from somewhere you'll never see, made by people you'll never meet. Now read chapter eighteen of the Apocalypse, and you'll find almost the same list. Gold, silver, pearls, silk, scarlet, ivory, cinnamon, perfume, wine, oil, fine flour, cattle, horses, chariots. It's the shipping manifest of that great city, Babylon. And everyone who traded in it is standing at a distance, crying, because the city is gone.
screen: `SCROLLING A SHOPPING APP.` → `THE SAME LIST, IN THE APOCALYPSE.` → `THE CITY IS GONE.`

segments.voice: In the Apocalypse, Babylon is a code name, and a long line of readers have taken it as Rome: chapter seventeen speaks of seven mountains, and Rome was rich, powerful, and hard on the people who wouldn't bow to it. The first letter of Peter seems to use the same code, sending greetings from the church in Babylon. In chapter eighteen an angel lights up the earth with his glory and cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen." Then a voice from heaven: "Go out from her, my people; that you be not partakers of her sins." And then three groups of mourners. Kings, who lived in luxury with her. Merchants, who got rich off her. Sailors, who carried her cargo. They all stand far off, afraid, saying the same thing: in one hour. In one hour her judgment came; in one hour her riches were laid waste. Three times the text says it. Listen to the merchants' list again, all the way to the end. After the horses and chariots, the last items are bodies and human souls. People, bought and sold like the cinnamon. That's what the luxury was standing on. Then an angel picks up a stone like a great millstone and throws it into the sea: like that, Babylon will be thrown down and found no more. No more music in her streets. No more lamps. No more bride and bridegroom. The chapter isn't against beauty or trade. It's about a whole way of life that forgot people were not merchandise, and how fast it can vanish. Catholic social teaching makes a similar warning.
screen: `BABYLON: A CODE NAME FOR ROME.` · `GO OUT FROM HER, MY PEOPLE.` · `IN ONE HOUR, LAID WASTE.` · `THE LIST ENDS WITH HUMAN SOULS.` · then, large: `BABYLON THE GREAT IS FALLEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: buy one fewer thing. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind the last few things you bought or were about to buy. Picture them in a row. Pick one you don't really need, the one that was more about the scroll than the need. Now imagine not buying it. Notice whether anything in you protests, and let it protest. Then think about who made the things you do buy: the hands, the fields, the factories, the drivers. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, just hold them in mind for a moment, people, not merchandise. The bell holds the time.
Babylon falls. Apocalypse eighteen: the great city of luxury, built on bought and sold lives, laid waste in one hour. Today's word.
Your line: what doesn't last. Today, skip the purchase you chose, and give the money or the time to someone who needs it. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

629.title: The supper of the Lamb (Apocalypse 19:6–9)
629.hook: blessed are they that are called: echoed at every Mass
629.howItsDone: Before Communion at every Mass, the priest shows the host and says Behold the Lamb of God, adding that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed; the people respond with the centurion's words, Lord, I am not worthy, and the Church teaches that the Eucharist anticipates the wedding feast of the Lamb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babylon falls, in one hour, and the merchants weep. Your line was what doesn't last. What did you skip buying, and where did it go instead? Day six hundred twenty-nine.

Alleluia is sung at Mass all year, except in Lent. It's in hymns, on Easter cards, in the names of choirs. Now look for it in the Apocalypse. In chapter nineteen it comes four times, close together. Right after Babylon falls, the noise of the merchants weeping is drowned out by another sound. John hears what sounds like a great crowd, like many waters, like great thunders, and they're shouting alleluia. Then they say why. There's going to be a wedding.
screen: `ALLELUIA, ALL YEAR LONG.` → `FOUR TIMES IN APOCALYPSE NINETEEN.` → `THERE'S GOING TO BE A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: The crowd sings that the Lord God Almighty reigns. Let us be glad and rejoice, they say, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready. She's given fine linen to wear, bright and clean, and the text explains the linen: it's the good deeds of the saints. So the bride is the Church, God's people, dressed in the love they've lived. Babylon was the city dressed in purple and scarlet, bought and sold. The bride is dressed in deeds. Then an angel tells John to write something down. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And the angel adds: these are the true words of God. Again and again in the Bible, God's love for his people is pictured as a marriage, from the prophets to Jesus's parable of the wedding feast. Here that picture becomes a feast. Now here's where Catholics hear it. At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest holds up the host and says, behold the Lamb of God. And then he says that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed. In Latin the line is beati qui ad cenam Agni vocati sunt: blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb. The people answer with the words of a centurion from Matthew's Gospel: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, as the Douay-Rheims gives it. Called, and not worthy, and coming anyway. The Church teaches that every Mass is a foretaste of this wedding feast.
screen: `ALLELUIA: THE LORD REIGNS.` · `THE BRIDE DRESSED IN DEEDS.` · `WRITE IT DOWN: BLESSED ARE THEY.` · `BEHOLD THE LAMB, AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT ARE CALLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear it ahead of time. Sit comfortably and breathe. Picture the moment at Mass just before Communion: the priest lifting the host, the quiet in the church, the words, behold the Lamb of God. Then the line about those who are called to the supper. Imagine hearing it as an invitation with your name on it, to a wedding feast that is already being set. Notice what comes up. If you pray, you can answer in the centurion's words, Lord, I am not worthy, but only say the word. If you don't, just sit with being invited. The bell holds the time.
Cenam Agni. Latin for the supper of the Lamb, the words said at every Mass just before Communion is offered. Today's word.
Your line: called to the supper. Today, when someone invites you anywhere, even for coffee, let it remind you of the other invitation. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

630.title: All things new (Apocalypse 21:1–5)
630.hook: God shall wipe away every tear
630.carry: behold, I make all things new
630.howItsDone: Apocalypse 21 is among the readings families may choose for a Catholic funeral Mass, and the Church teaches that at the end of time the whole universe will be renewed, with God dwelling among his people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alleluia, a wedding, and cenam Agni, the supper of the Lamb. Your line was called to the supper. Did you hear the invitation behind the words? Day six hundred thirty.

A kid falls off a bike on the sidewalk. Scraped knee, gravel in the palm, a howl you can hear three houses away. A parent comes running, kneels down on the concrete, and before the bandage, before anything, does one thing: takes the child's face in both hands and wipes the tears off with a thumb. You have to be very close to do it. Near the end of the Apocalypse, after the dragon and the beasts and Babylon, John says God will do exactly that.
screen: `A SCRAPED KNEE ON THE SIDEWALK.` → `A THUMB ACROSS A WET CHEEK.` → `GOD WILL DO EXACTLY THAT.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth." And the sea is no more. Some readers hear the sea as a picture of chaos, and John, remember, was on an island, cut off by water. No more of that. Then: "And I John saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." Notice the direction. The city comes down. The story doesn't end with people escaping earth to somewhere else. It ends with heaven coming to earth. A great voice says: "Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them." The Greek word behind tabernacle is the word for a tent: God pitching his tent among his people, the same image John's Gospel uses when it says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And Catholics call the place in church where the Eucharist is kept the tabernacle. Then the line from the hook: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more, for the former things are passed away." Not prevent the tears. Wipe them. The tears were real. And then the one on the throne speaks: "Behold, I make all things new." Read it slowly. Not I make all new things, a replacement world, the old one thrown out. All things, made new. The Catechism teaches that the universe itself will be renewed, not discarded. The Church offers this among the readings at funerals. Families sit in the front pew with tears that haven't been wiped yet, and they hear what's promised.
screen: `A NEW HEAVEN AND A NEW EARTH.` · `THE CITY COMES DOWN.` · `GOD PITCHES HIS TENT WITH US.` · `NOT ALL NEW THINGS: ALL THINGS NEW.` · then, large: `GOD SHALL WIPE AWAY ALL TEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wipe someone's tears, or your own. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is crying right now, or who has been sad for a long time: a friend grieving, a child, a parent, a stranger in the news. Picture yourself kneeling beside them, close, and gently wiping their face. Then, if there's a sorrow of your own, let someone do the same for you. You can even touch your own cheek with your thumb. If you pray, you can rest in the promise: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes. If you don't, just let the gentleness stay. The bell holds the time.
Tabernacle, a tent. Apocalypse twenty-one: God pitching his tent among his people, in the new Jerusalem come down to earth. Today's word.

Your line: behold, I make all things new. Today, comfort one person in some small, close way. And that's week ninety: they rest not, worthy is the lamb, every tongue, clothed with the sun, what doesn't last, called to the supper, and all things new. Day six hundred thirty.

original.note: Greek: I make all things new (Apocalypse 21:5). kainos means new in kind, fresh.

trapdoor: what you thought: heaven is somewhere else, far away from this world.
what it means: heaven comes down; God dwells with his people; this world, renewed, with every tear wiped away.
what a scholar hears: kainos, new in quality, not just in time; and skēnē, tent, God pitching his tent with us, as in John 1:14.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1042–1047; Order of Christian Funerals, readings
